title: Second Homily on the Day of the Dormition

pairs.en: *“And the tomb becomes a ladder to heaven!”* (First sticheron at Vespers)

sections.heading: A ladder to heaven — or to hell

pairs.en: It becomes a ladder to heaven — and it becomes one to hell! How many people pass along this ladder daily and hourly! Yet how many are there of whom we can say with firm assurance that they are in heaven? One might conclude from this that whether a man passes through the tomb to heaven or to hell does not depend on those who pass through it at all — that it lies in the will of some being, not equally well-disposed toward everyone, who to please his own caprice appoints some to ascend through the tomb into heaven and others to descend through that same tomb into hell. And yet, brethren, this momentous matter depends entirely on the man himself! It is fully within his own will to turn the ladder of the tomb wherever he pleases — upward or downward, to heaven or to hell!
And do we ourselves turn it toward hell?.. for our own selves?.. for all eternity?.. Who would believe it, if unceasing experience did not bear witness to it in the most incontestable way!

sections.heading: How the ladder is built unnoticed

pairs.en: How, then, does this — one may say without exaggeration — miracle come about? How does man, a creature so self-loving, who lives precisely so that things may always go well for him — how does he reach such forgetfulness of his own interests that the ladder given him for ascending to heaven he turns irrevocably toward hell? All this happens, brethren, in the most imperceptible way, and this very imperceptibility is in part the reason why a man acts against his own good. The tomb shows itself to be a ladder at the moment of death itself, but it is being made a ladder throughout the whole of life — and it becomes one unnoticed. A man lives without thinking of his tomb; but the tomb, on the contrary, always remembers him, and every action of his is turned into a rung of the ladder: the good, toward heaven; the evil, toward hell. And so, when he dies, a man finds the ladder of the tomb already finished — built imperceptibly by his own hands during his life. Often he sees with horror that the whole of it is turned downward, into hell; but he no longer has the power to turn it toward heaven — no one lives a second time — and the unhappy soul goes where its terrible ladder leads it!

sections.heading: As the life, so the death

pairs.en: Yes, brethren: as the life is, so is the death! Strictly speaking, it is not the tomb that becomes the ladder, but our deeds. He who has lived in love toward God and his neighbours will find, in death also, the love of God and of his neighbours toward himself. But he who has passed his life in the mire of sin, has been cold toward what is good, and has not managed to wash away his corruption with the tears of repentance, will find nothing in death but darkness, cold, and decay. The coffin of such a man, as it is lowered into the ground, will not come to rest in peace in the earth's motherly embrace, but will sink down to the very depths of hell. Such is the law of our existence: good done here produces good there also; evil done here drags evil after it there as well. Shall we complain that our salvation has thus been handed into our own hands and made to depend on our deeds? But in this very thing lies the high privilege of our nature; this is the very thing that makes us, the earthborn, equal to the Angels. The wisdom and almighty power of God have made the impossible possible: the tomb, built by our sins and by its very essence a dwelling place of nothing but corruption, has been turned into a ladder by which one may ascend from earth to heaven. But which way to turn this ladder — that had to remain in our power: without it we would cease to be human beings.

Remembering this, let us live with death in view, so that in dying we may behold life. Let us not grow slack in doing good works without ceasing, however much toil they may cost, in the firm assurance that each of them will one day serve us as a rung toward heaven — and the harder it was, the greater the height to which it will raise us. Let us flee with all diligence from every vice, however beautiful it may appear, remembering that in time it will turn into a rung toward hell.

If we, like the Most Holy Virgin, whose all-honoured falling asleep we bless today, pass our life in keeping the commandments of God, in purity of spirit and body — or manage to recover our lost purity through faith in the Redeemer and heartfelt contrition for our sins — then on the day of our own falling asleep a wondrous miracle will be worked upon us also: our tomb, too, will be for us a ladder to heaven. Amen.
